title: InfinityStar: Uniﬁed Spacetime AutoRegressive Modeling for Visual Generatio

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Eq. (2) defines p(r_1^1, ..., r_K^N) = ∏_{c=1}^N ∏_{k=1}^K p(r_k^c | r_1^c, ..., r_{k-1}^c, ψ(t)). This makes every clip independent of all previous clips, because the conditioning set contains only tokens from the same clip. This directly contradicts the preceding sentence that clips are generated sequentially conditioned on prior clip predictions, and it omits the cross-clip/temporal autoregression central to the method. The condition should include previous-clip tokens, e.g. r^{<c}, or at least the attended last-scale tokens of the preceding clip.

The Abstract states that the model generates a 5s 720p video 'approximately 10× faster than leading diffusion-based methods.' Table 6 reports Wan 2.1 at 1864 s and InfinityStar at 58 s, which is a 32× speedup; the also-listed Nova comparison gives 354 s vs 58 s, about a 6× speedup. No baseline in the paper supports the 10× figure, and the claim is at least unsupported/inconsistent with the paper's own latency table.

The Abstract says InfinityStar is 'among the first discrete autoregressive video generators capable of producing high-quality 720p videos,' while the Introduction claims 'InfinityStar is the first discrete autoregressive model capable of generating high-quality videos.' These statements are internally contradictory, and the unqualified 'first' claim is not substantiated given earlier discrete autoregressive video models such as Emu3 are discussed in the paper itself.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract / Introduction vs Tables 1 and 2 / Section 4.3
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The headline VBench result (83.74, 'surpassing industry-leading HunyuanVideo') is obtained with prompt rewriting, as marked by the † footnote, while HunyuanVideo and several other baselines are not marked as using prompt rewriting. The paper also admits that 'other baselines have variable usage of prompt enhancements.' Because prompt rewriting can substantially affect VBench and GenEval alignment scores, the direct superiority claims in the Abstract and Introduction are misleading without a controlled comparison or caveat.

The paper cites the VBench benchmark as [38] 'Evaluation Agent: Efficient and Promptable Evaluation Framework for Visual Generative Models.' VBench is actually the benchmark from Huang et al., 'VBench: Comprehensive Benchmark Suite for Video Generative Models' (CVPR 2024). Reference [38] is a separate follow-up/evaluation-agent paper and is the wrong source for the VBench benchmark.

Table 2 lists 'VideoCrafter-2.0 [5]', but reference [5] is titled 'VideoCrafter1: Open Diffusion Models for High-Quality Video Generation.' VideoCrafter 2.0 is a distinct work and should not be cited to the VideoCrafter 1 paper.

The text states that mainstream discrete video tokenizers are 'either trained from scratch [1] or starting from a pretrained discrete image tokenizer [35, 29].' The cited works [35] (MAGVITv2 / 'Language Model Beats Diffusion') and [29] (OmniTokenizer) are not examples of initializing from a pretrained discrete image tokenizer; they are video/joint image-video tokenizers trained as tokenizers themselves. The attribution appears incorrect.

Reproducibility-critical training details are omitted or left unspecified: exact data splits and statistics for the 221M image+video and 16M video corpora, optimizer momentum and weight decay, global batch sizes, learning-rate schedules, warm-up, and gradient clipping. The paper itself states that several of these are 'unspecified'/'not reported,' and the provided few hyperparameters are insufficient to reproduce the training protocol.
